Modular segregation of task-dependent brain networks contributes to the
development of executive function in children
Chunjie Wang, Yuzheng Hu, Jian Weng, Feiyan Chen, Huafeng Liu

NeuroImage 206 (2020) 116334
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2019.116334
© 2019 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Inc. This is an open access article under the CC BY-NC-ND license.

Executive function (EF) refers as to a set of high-level cognitive abilities that are critical to many aspects of daily
life. Despite its importance in human daily life, the neural networks responsible for the development of EF in
childhood are not well understood. The present study thus aimed to examine the development of task-dependent
brain network organization and its relationship to age-related improvements in EF.

Eighty-eight children, ranging in age from 7 to 12, were recruited
from a single district within Qiqihar city, Heilongjiang Province. This
study was approved by the research ethics review board of Zhejiang
University in China, and was conducted in accordance with the guide-
lines of Helsinki Declaration. Informed consent was obtained from both
the children and their parents. All participants were from urban families.
They had normal hearing, normal or corrected-to-normal vision, no
history of neurological or psychiatric disorder, and no reports of special
educational assistance requirements. Six children were excluded because
of behavioral data missing; fifteen children were excluded because of
excessive head motion during fMRI scanning (exceeding 3.0 mm in
displacement or 3° in rotation), yielding sixty-seven children in the final
sample (38 boys, mean age = 10.03 ± 1.57, range = 7.18–12.48). Intel-
ligence, as assessed by the Chinese version of Combined Raven’s Matrices
Test, ranged from 86 to 127 (mean intelligence = 108 ± 9).

Imaging was performed on a 1.5 T Philips MRI scanner with a stan-
dard eight-channel head coil. For each participant, a high-resolution
brain structural image was obtained using a 3-dimensional fast field
echo (FFE) sequence (TR = 25 ms, TE = 4.6 ms, flip angle = 15°, 150
slices in the sagittal plane, FOV = 256 × 256 mm2, matrix
size = 256 × 256). Functional images were acquired using a single-shot
echo-planar imaging (EPI) sequence (TR = 2000 ms, TE = 50 ms, flip
angle = 90°, 22 interleaved ascending slices per volume, slice thickness = 5 mm, slice gap = 0.8 mm, FOV = 230 × 230 mm2,
matrix size = 64 × 64).

The Dots task adapted from Davidson et al. (2006) was used to
measure EF in this study. Using this task paradigm, our prior work has
observed significant age-related improvements in EF performance over
the age of 7–12 year old. In this task, two different task conditions
(single-task and mixed-task) were designed to probe EF ability.
The single-task condition included two types of blocks (single-congruent
and single-incongruent). The single-congruent blocks presented only
stripped dots, and subjects were instructed to respond on the same side as
the stripped dots. The single-incongruent blocks presented only gray
dots, and subjects were instructed to respond on the opposite side to the
gray dots. The mixed-task condition randomly presented stripped or gray
dots, and subjects were instructed to make the side-congruent or
side-incongruent responses according to which types of dots were pre-
sented (e.g. stripped same side, gray opposite side).

A block design was used in the fMRI experiment with two sessions of
scanning. During each session, there were three blocks presenting only
stripped dots (single-task), three blocks presenting only gray dots (single-
task), and three blocks randomly presenting stripped and gray dots
(mixed-task). Each block had a 26-s task condition, followed by a 12-s
fixation slide. The 26-s task condition included a 2-s task instruction
and twelve 2-s trials. In each trial, a fixation was presented on the screen
for 500 ms; subsequently, a stripped or gray dot was displayed on the left
or right side of the fixation for 750 ms or disappeared if a response was
given; finally, a blank interval was presented for a variable duration in
order to keep each trial last for 2 s. There was also a 10-s pre-scan
performed before each task session to obtain a stable signal. Thus, the
scanning duration for the whole task-state was 704 s, resulting in 352
functional volumes.

For each participant, accuracy (ACC) and mean response time (RT) of
correct trials were calculated separately for the single-task and mixed-
task conditions. Trials with RT shorter than 200 ms were assumed to
be too fast to indicate a reasonable respond and were not included in ACC
or RT calculations. To avoid confounds from non-EF cognitive
processes, EF ability in this study was tested by introducing the difference
scores of ACC (ACCsingle-task – ACCmixed-task) and RT (RTmixed-task – RTsingle-
task) between the two task conditions.

The imaging data were preprocessed using the Data Processing As-
sistant for Resting-state fMRI Advanced Edition (DPARSF-A, version 4.3)
toolbox. Preprocessing steps included discarding the five
pre-scans, slice-timing correction, and head-motion correction. Then the
functional images were aligned to the corresponding T1-weighted im-
ages, and were normalized to the MNI space with a resampling voxel size
of 3 × 3 × 3 mm3. Finally, the functional images were smoothed using a
6 mm full-width half-maximum (FWHM) Gaussian kernel. Frame-wise
displacement (FD) was used to characterize head motion
inside the scanner. A censoring/scrubbing strategy was used
to remove time points with FD greater than 0.3 mm. Task-dependent
functional connectivity was assessed using the CONN toolbox.
For each participant, the five components of white-matter and
cerebrospinal fluid signals, the six motion parameters and their first-
order derivatives, and global signal time courses were extracted and
regressed out from the data. Task-induced neural effects were removed
using separate block regressors convolved with a canonical hemodynamic
response function and their first-derivative terms. A high pass filter with
a cut-off frequency of 0.01 Hz was also implemented for the imaging data.

To obtain defined nodes, we applied a functional template as pro-
posed in a previous study. This functional template can parcellate the
brain into 160 functionally segregated regions of interest (ROIs) that
cover most of the cerebral cortex and cerebellum. The set of ROIs (6 mm
diameter spheres) were generated using the peak coordinates derived
from a series of meta-analyses of fMRI activation studies. Average time
courses from each ROI were extracted and pair-wise Pearson correlation
coefficients were computed between these ROIs. To enable comparison
of network properties across participants, we used a proportional
threshold to ensure the same number of network edges for each partici-
pant. In the present study, we chose a sparsity threshold of 15%.

All graph theory measures were calculated using the Brain Connectiv-
ity Toolbox. The 160 ROIs have been assigned into six
functional modules, corresponding to the default-mode network (DMN),
frontal–parietal network (FPN), cingulo-opercular network (CONN),
sensorimotor network (SMN), visual network, and the cerebellum. In
order to quantify the degree of modular segregation, participation coeffi-
cient (PC) was calculated. In addition to PC, we also calculated the
number of connections within each module, and the number of connec-
tions between any two pairs of modules.

Partial correlation analyses were used to examine the associ-
ations between age, task performance and brain network properties.
Gender, intelligence and head motion (characterized by mean FD) were
used as covariates in the partial correlation analyses. Finally, we per-
formed an exploratory mediation analysis to test whether the brain
network measures could explain age-related improvements in EF perfor-
mance. The significance of the mediation effect was
evaluated using the PROCESS macro for SPSS 22.0. This
approach can generate a 95% bootstrapped confidence interval from
repeated resampling (10,000 samples) of the observed data.

Supplementary data to this article can be found online at the journal website.
